VIABILITY: The path to revenue is clear in form but unproven in substance. A $9/month subscription for a narrow, real pain point (offline sales logging and tax estimation) is simple and plausible, and the problem evidence (17 of 23 vendors on paper, 12 of 23 unsure of tax owed) is credible primary research. However, validation is thin: 12 free-trial users and one paying customer ($27 total revenue) is a single data point on willingness to pay. No conversion rate, retention, or churn has been observed. The honey-and-preserves vendor may not be representative.

UNIT ECONOMICS AND SCALE OF THE PRIZE: At $9/month, revenue per vendor is ~$108/year. The stated local ceiling of 180 payers (~$19,400 ARR) is too small to sustain even one salary, and the 100-vendor, 12-month goal implies ~$10,800 ARR against $18,000 of projected costs, so the plan as stated does not break even. Even the national figure (85,000 'serious' vendors) yields only ~$9M ARR at 100% penetration, which makes this a niche lifestyle-scale business unless pricing, scope, or revenue streams expand. Seasonality (many markets run 6-8 months) further threatens retention under a monthly subscription; the founders themselves flag this and do not yet have an answer (annual or seasonal pricing is an obvious test).

ASSUMPTION VALIDITY: (1) The 15% conversion of reached vendors is an unsupported guess, and 'reached' is undefined; typical free-to-paid conversion in SMB apps is often lower. (2) The market sizing is acknowledged as unvalidated; the 30 vendors/market average and one-third 'serious' share are guesses, and counting vendors across multiple markets inflates stall-based estimates. (3) Customer acquisition cost is unmeasured, which is critical when each customer yields ~$108/year and acquisition is via in-person market visits (high touch, low density). (4) Manager-paid aggregate reports are speculative and untested, and could raise vendor privacy concerns. (5) The sample of 23 vendors at three markets near one university is small and geographically clustered.

COMPETITION AND DEFENSIBILITY: The moat is weak. Established POS and accounting tools already offer offline modes, reporting, and tax features, and typically accept card payments, which is a major gap since many vendors need integrated card processing. Square-type products are free to start and make money on payment processing, a model Ledgerleaf cannot match at $9/month without card integration. Ledgerleaf's advantage (simplicity and focus) is real but easily copied, and there is no proprietary technology or network effect. Card payment integration, funded at only $3,500, may be a prerequisite for adoption rather than an enhancement, and could shift the model toward transaction-fee revenue, which is likely the stronger monetization path.

SCALABILITY: Software distribution is cheap, but acquisition here is local and relational. Partnerships with market associations could provide a scalable channel and are the most promising growth lever. Product-side scalability looks fine (offline-first with sync is solid architecture), but go-to-market scalability is unproven.

EXECUTION RISK: Team is complementary (domain experience, engineering, accounting logic) and the plan shows unusual self-awareness about its unknowns. Weaknesses are part-time student commitment (~15 hrs/week each), no legal entity yet, and possible tax/liability exposure from giving tax estimates without disclaimers or accuracy validation across jurisdictions (local rates entered manually, which is error-prone).

USE OF FUNDS: The ask is well-aligned with learning goals: the $1,000 willingness-to-pay survey and ten-market pilot directly target the biggest unknowns, and legal formation is sensible. The plan is honest that the end goal is determining whether the business can reach sustainable revenue.

OVERALL: A credible, well-framed early experiment with a real problem and honest uncertainty, but the current model likely produces too little revenue per customer to be a venture-scale or even self-sustaining business without pricing changes, card-processing revenue, or broader vendor-segment expansion. Fundable as a low-cost validation project; viability hinges on measured conversion, retention through seasonality, and a stronger monetization and differentiation story against incumbents.

Business plan text:

Ledgerleaf
Ledgerleaf: Executive Summary
Problem
Farmers' market vendors run small cash-and-card businesses from temporary stalls, often in
locations with poor or no internet service. In conversations with 23 vendors at three markets
near our university, 17 told us they record sales on paper or in a notebook and transfer the
figures to a spreadsheet or to a bookkeeper days later. Twelve said they had at some point been
unsure how much sales tax they owed for a given month. Paper tallies are easy to lose, and
errors made while a line of customers waits are hard to catch afterward. The cost to a vendor
is small per day but recurs every market day: time spent reconciling totals in the evening, and
the risk of under- or over-reporting tax.
Solution
Ledgerleaf is an application for phones and tablets that works fully without a connection. A
vendor sets up a short list of items and prices, taps to record each sale, and notes whether
payment was cash or card. All data is stored on the device. When the device reaches a network,
Ledgerleaf syncs the records to a secure account and backs them up. At the end of each market
day the app shows total sales, sales by item, and the sales tax collected based on the vendor's
local rate, which the vendor enters during setup. A monthly view gives a running estimate of
tax owed so the vendor can set money aside. The interface is deliberately limited to a few
large buttons so it can be used with one hand while serving customers.
Market
We estimate there are roughly 8,600 farmers' markets in the United States, based on publicly
reported directory counts. If an average market hosts 30 vendors, that suggests about 258,000
vendor stalls, though many vendors sell at more than one market and some are hobbyists with
little revenue. We believe a reasonable first target is full-time and serious part-time
vendors, which we guess to be perhaps a third of the total, or around 85,000. We have not yet
validated these figures with an independent source and treat them as rough. Our first target is
the 40 markets within a two-hour drive of our university, representing roughly 1,200 vendors.
Business Model
Ledgerleaf will charge a subscription of $9 per month per vendor, with a free tier limited to
one market day per week of stored history. If we convert 15 percent of vendors reached in our
local region, that would be about 180 paying vendors and roughly $19,400 in annual recurring
revenue. We also see potential to charge market managers for aggregated reports on vendor
activity, though we have not tested whether managers would pay for this. Customer acquisition
will rely on visits to markets, word of mouth among vendors, and partnerships with market
associations. We have not yet measured acquisition cost.
Competition
Vendors currently use paper notebooks, general spreadsheets, and general-purpose point-of-sale
and accounting products. Several of these products offer some offline capability, and many
include sales reporting and tax features. Ledgerleaf differs by focusing narrowly on farmers'
market workflows and by being simpler to operate at the stall. We recognize that a larger
provider could add similar features, and that our product does not yet take card payments
directly, which some competitors do. Our current advantage is focus and ease of use rather than
any proprietary technology.
Team
Maribel Okonkwo-Reyes, chief executive, is a senior in business administration who spent two
summers working a family stall at a regional market and conducted the vendor interviews. Tobias

Lindqvist-Hart, chief technology officer, is a senior in computer science and built the
application, including its local storage and sync logic. Daniela Whitcombe, head of operations,
is a junior in accounting who designed the tax estimation logic and the end-of-day report. All
three founders are full-time students and work on Ledgerleaf alongside their coursework,
averaging about 15 hours per week each.
Milestones and Financials
To date we have defined the core concept, registered the business name, built a working version
of the application, and launched a website describing the product. Twelve vendors are using the
product in a free trial, and one vendor, a honey and preserves seller, has paid for a
subscription at $9 per month. Total revenue to date is $27. Our spending to date is
approximately $640, funded personally by the founders, covering website hosting, a developer
account for app distribution, and printed signage. We have not yet formed a legal entity for
the venture and operate informally; incorporation is an early use of any funds we receive. Over
the next twelve months we project reaching 100 paying vendors, though this depends on
conversion from trial users, which we have not yet observed at scale. Our principal costs would
be part-time contract development, app store fees, and travel to markets, which we estimate at
$18,000 for the year.
What We Ask For
We are requesting $15,000 in competition funding. We would allocate $4,000 to legal formation
and basic accounting setup, $6,500 to expanding the pilot to ten markets including vendor
onboarding visits, $3,500 to contract development for card payment integration, and $1,000 to a
vendor survey to better measure willingness to pay and acquisition cost. Beyond funding, we
would value mentorship on pricing, on how to approach market associations, and on whether a
subscription model is appropriate for vendors with highly seasonal income. Our goal at the end
of the funding period is to demonstrate paid retention across several markets and to determine
whether the business can reach sustainable revenue.

Question: Comment on the viability and scalability of the business model and strategy. Address whether the company has a clear path to making money and growing, and evaluate the validity of the entrepreneur's assumptions.
